scene.bubble: We're reading To Kill a Mockingbird. Review your grammar and learn to punctuate for effect.
scene.intro: Our reading club has reached To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee, a novel about justice, fairness and speaking up for others. In this unit you read about a famous trial, you review the grammar of earlier units, and you learn to use dashes and commas for effect in your writing. A well-placed dash — like this one — can make a reader stop and think. Let's give your sentences a stronger voice.

activities.title: Reading — a trial and a brave choice

data.title: To Kill a Mockingbird: standing up for what is right
data.author: mateo
data.text:
This month our reading club is discussing To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee. It is narrated by Scout, a curious young girl who watches her small town struggle with prejudice.

Her father, Atticus, is a lawyer — a calm, principled man — who agrees to defend an innocent person that most people have already judged. It is not a popular choice. Yet Atticus does it anyway, because his conscience will not let him look away.

The trial is the heart of the book. The evidence is clear, the witnesses contradict each other, and the truth seems obvious — but fairness does not win easily. Nadia was moved by one line: “Courage, real courage, is knowing you are beaten before you begin, and starting anyway.”

In our discussion, Liam made a simple point. “The book is not only about a trial,” he said. “It is about listening — really listening — to people who are different from us.”

Harper Lee teaches us that justice needs voices. When something is wrong, someone must stand up, speak clearly, and refuse to stay silent.

data.title: Punctuation for effect: dashes and commas
data.intro: Good writers use punctuation to control the reader's attention. A dash adds a dramatic pause or an extra idea; a pair of commas adds extra, non-essential information smoothly.

examples.text: Atticus defends Tom — a brave, unpopular choice.
Scout, curious as ever, watches everything.
The truth was clear — yet the jury did not listen.
Courage, real courage, means standing alone.

rules: Use a dash ( — ) to add a dramatic pause or an extra idea at the end of a sentence.
Use a pair of commas to add extra, non-essential information in the middle of a sentence.
Do not overuse dashes; one strong dash has more effect than many.

practice.instructions: Choose the best option to complete each sentence.

items.sentence: Atticus made his choice ___ he would defend an innocent man.
Scout, ___ as ever, followed the whole trial.
We use a pair of ___ to add extra, non-essential information.
Review: Justice ___ not always been served in the story.
Review: During the trial an innocent man ___ being judged unfairly.

activities.title: Open cloze — review the novel. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.text: In the novel, an innocent man {1} being judged by the whole town. The trial {2} been watched by curious children. Justice has not {3} done fairly here. Atticus knows the verdict {4} have been different. If people {5} really listened, the outcome would have changed. Real courage, {6} Atticus shows, means standing alone.

Notice how Harper Lee uses simple words to show deep ideas. For Thursday, choose one moment that shows real bravery. Read closely, and always think about fairness.

activities.title: Speaking — justice and voice. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, talk about justice, fairness and speaking up. Model: “When is it important to speak up?” — “It is important to speak up when someone is treated unfairly, even if it is hard.” 1) Why does Atticus defend an innocent man? 2) Is it easy to be brave when others disagree? 3) When have you seen someone stand up for what is right? 4) How can students make their school fairer? Then record your best answers.

homework.prompt: Write 6–8 sentences about justice, fairness or a brave choice in To Kill a Mockingbird. Use at least one dash and one pair of commas for effect, for example: 'Courage, real courage, means standing alone' and 'The truth was clear — yet nobody listened'. Capital letters and full stops!

Discuss justice, fairness and speaking up for others (B1 Speaking).
Read about a trial and follow how ideas connect in a gapped text (B1 Reading).
Use dashes and commas for effect and review earlier grammar in writing.
Punctuation for effect (dashes and commas); review of passives and modals; vocabulary of justice and fairness.
